An assassin is a person who deliberately and secretly kills a specific, carefully chosen target — almost always someone who is important, powerful, or well-known, such as a political leader, a president, a king, a general, or a public figure.

The killing is never random or accidental. It is always planned in advance, and the assassin always has a specific reason for choosing that particular victim.
What Makes an Assassin Different from a "Murderer" or a "Killer"

This is the most important thing to understand, because these words seem similar but are not the same.

A murderer is simply anyone who illegally kills another person. The victim could be a stranger, a neighbor, or a family member — anyone at all. There may be no planning involved; it could be a sudden act of rage.

A killer is even broader — it refers to anyone or anything that causes death.

An assassin, however, is far more specific. Three things almost always define an assassin:

1. The target is important. Assassins do not kill ordinary, unknown people. Their targets are figures who hold power, influence, or fame — presidents, prime ministers, generals, activists, celebrities, or other high-profile individuals. This is a near-universal feature of the word.

2. The act is premeditated. An assassin plans the killing carefully and deliberately. It is never impulsive. The assassin studies the target, picks the moment, and executes the act with intention.

3. There is a motive beyond personal anger. An assassin kills for a purpose bigger than a personal grudge. The motive is usually one of these:

  • Political — to remove a leader, change the direction of a government, or make a political statement.
  • Financial — the assassin was hired and paid to kill the target (this person is often also called a hired assassin or a contract killer).
  • Ideological or religious — the assassin kills because of a deeply held belief or cause.
The Sense of Secrecy and Skill

Another quality the word carries is stealth and calculated precision. An assassin is not someone who charges into a battle. An assassin typically operates in the shadows — quietly, cleverly, and with skill. The word itself suggests a certain cold, methodical professionalism, even when the assassin is not a paid professional. There is always an element of cunning and concealment.

This is why, in history, the word is associated with figures who struck unexpectedly — appearing from nowhere, completing their mission, and disappearing.

These examples will sharpen your understanding:

  • The men who killed Julius Caesar in 44 BC were assassins. Their target was the most powerful man in Rome, their act was carefully planned by a group of conspirators, and their motive was political — they wanted to save the Roman Republic.
  • Abraham Lincoln was killed by John Wilkes Booth in 1865. Booth was an assassin — he targeted the President of the United States, planned the attack deliberately, and acted out of political and ideological motivation.
  • Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was assassinated in 1914 — an event that triggered World War I. The killers were politically motivated nationalists who specifically chose him as their target.

In all these cases, notice the pattern: a prominent target, a plan, and a purpose.

The word also lives in a very common figurative phrase: character assassination. Here, no one is physically killed. Instead, someone deliberately and systematically destroys another person's reputation, honor, or public image — through lies, rumors, or a smear campaign. The person doing this could informally be called a character assassin.

This figurative meaning works because it borrows the core idea of the word — a deliberate, targeted act of destruction against a specific, prominent person — and applies it to reputation rather than life.
In Fiction, Games, and Popular Culture

In movies, novels, and video games, the word "assassin" is used very widely for any highly skilled, stealthy killer who operates alone and is hired to kill specific targets. The word has become a genre and archetype of its own. You will see characters described as assassins even when their targets are not political figures, simply because they are professional, secretive, and precise killers for hire. This usage is somewhat looser than the strict definition, but it is entirely standard and widely understood.
An assassin is a person who deliberately and secretly kills a specific, prominent or important individual — always with planning, and almost always for a political, financial, or ideological purpose.
